title: TC1-04873
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal.

The Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Bangladesh. He fears persecution in Bangladesh at the hands of the Awami League (AL) and the Chatra League (CL) due to his opposition to their extortion attempts and his refusal to hand over his father's business. In XXXX 2017, a local CL leader demanded the Appellant's father pay XXXX lakh as a "subscription". When his father refused, five or six CL "goons" came to the Appellant's home and threatened his mother. When the Appellant and his father returned home, they were also threatened. They attempted to report the situation to police, but the police told them to remove the name of the CL members from their complaint. The Appellant continued to receive threats and, at the insistence of his father, left Bangladesh and came to study in Canada as a means to escape.
The Appellant arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX 2018. He filed his claim for refugee protection on 27 January 2020. RPD findings

The RPD found that due to discrepancies between the Appellant's Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative, his documents, and his testimony, the Appellant was, on a balance of probabilities, not credible. It found this was determinative of the Appellant's claim. Appellant's submissions

The Appellant's submissions lack precision and clarity. In essence, he argues that the RPD breached natural justice or procedural fairness. He also argues that the RPD's credibility findings are erroneous. New Evidence and Oral Hearing

According to the Law,1 I can only accept evidence that: (i) arose after the RPD decision; or (ii) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or (iii) that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.2

The Appellant asks that I admit the most recent United States Department of State's Country Report on Human Rights Practices for Bangladesh.3 I find there is no need to enter this document as it is already included in the most recent National Documentation Package (NDP) for Bangladesh.4
As no new evidence has been admitted, I have no jurisdiction to hold an oral hearing.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.5 The RPD did not breach natural justice or procedural fairness

The Appellant's submissions make several general allegations which, in essence, assert that he was denied natural justice. The Appellant argues that the RPD was biased, was aggressive in its questioning, and did not have sufficient knowledge of country conditions in Bangladesh. He argues the RPD failed to consider the chairperson's guidelines, the COVID-19 situation and the stress, psychological and emotional condition of the Appellant in assessing his claim.

Counsel for the Appellant does not point to any specific instance or evidence to support these assertions. I have reviewed the Record in its entirety and listened to the audio recording of the hearing. Although some of its questions were direct and pointed, I find no evidence of bias or of inappropriately aggressive questioning or tone of the part of the RPD nor its disregard of the Appellant's particular circumstances. On the contrary, I find the RPD clearly identified the credibility issues and provided the Appellant with an opportunity to respond to its concerns.

Although the Appellant does not identify which guideline he is referring to or how it should be applied to his case, I have nonetheless considered the Chairperson's Guideline on Procedures With Respect to Vulnerable Persons (the Guideline). The Guideline defines vulnerable persons as follows: 2. Definition of vulnerable persons 2.1 For the purposes of this guideline, vulnerable persons are individuals whose ability to present their cases before the IRB is severely impaired. Such persons may include, but would not be limited to, the mentally ill, minors, the elderly, victims of torture, survivors of genocide and crimes against humanity, women who have suffered gender-related persecution, and individuals who have been victims of persecution based on sexual orientation and gender identity. 2.2 The definition of vulnerable persons may apply to persons presenting a case before the IRB, namely, to refugee protection claimants (in the RPD), appellants (in the IAD and in the RAD), and persons concerned (in the ID). In certain circumstances, close family members of the vulnerable person who are also presenting their cases before the IRB may qualify as vulnerable persons because of the way in which they have been affected by their loved one's condition. 2.3 Persons who appear before the IRB frequently find the process difficult for various reasons, including language and cultural barriers and because they may have suffered traumatic experiences that resulted in some degree of vulnerability. IRB proceedings have been designed to recognize the very nature of the IRB's mandate, which inherently involves persons who may have some vulnerabilities. In all cases, the IRB takes steps to ensure the fairness of the proceedings. This guideline addresses difficulties that go beyond those that are common to most persons appearing before the IRB. It is intended to apply to individuals who face particular difficulty and who require special consideration in the procedural handling of their cases. It applies to the more severe cases of vulnerability. 2.4 Wherever it is reasonably possible, the vulnerability must be supported by independent credible evidence filed with the IRB Registry. [emphasis added, references omitted]6

In my review of the materials before me and before the RPD, I see no evidence to show that the Appellant is severely impaired or that he requires special consideration beyond that which is already inherent in the RPD's procedures. Although counsel for the Appellant asserts that "Due to Covid 19 the claimant could not do the psychological and emotional medical assessment of her (sic) present medical condition,"7 I find no basis for this submission. The Appellant was represented at his hearing and did not indicate that his ability to provide evidence was in any way impaired. On my review of the audio recording and transcript, it is evident that the Appellant understood the questions being asked and was able to answer accordingly. Although his answers may not have been satisfactory, this alone is not evidence either of an impairment or a denial of natural justice. Further, the Appellant's counsel provided submissions in writing subsequent to the hearing and did not raise any medical, psychological or other impairment which required special consideration.
The Appellant's arguments with respect to natural justice are therefore rejected. Overall, the RPD's credibility findings are correct

The Appellant asserts that the RPD's credibility findings are incorrect. Again, counsel for the Appellant does not point to any specific errors. Rather, he outlines several general principles without applying them to the facts or evidence of this case.

It is not for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to make arguments for the Appellant. However, given the inadequacy of the arguments submitted by counsel on the Appellant's behalf, I have found it necessary to consider each of the RPD's credibility findings to determine whether they are correct. While I disagree with some of the RPD's findings, I find that, overall, it did not err in its negative assessment of the Appellant's credibility or in assigning little weight to his documentation. Involvement of Minister S. not established

The RPD first found that the involvement of Minister S. in the attacks against the Appellant and his family was speculative. I agree. The Appellant's testimony was that in order for the agents of persecution to be able to attack the Appellant's house and business, they would need the support of a powerful person.8 The RPD did not err in finding this was speculative. Aside from this, there was no evidence of Minister S.'s, or any other government or AL, involvement. Omission from BOC not adequately explained

With respect to the attack on XXXX XXXX 2017, the Appellant testified that, "... my mother became unconscious and we took her to the hospital and I also had sustained cut injuries on my back after they beat me up with iron rods, so I also went to the clinic. My entire body had lot of blood marks and bruises because of the beating." 9 The Appellant provided a medical report to document his trip to the clinic.10 However, the Appellant's BOC indicates that, "My mother could not bear the trauma and she fainted due to hypertension. So, we immediately brought her to a nearby hospital for treatment and became busy taking care of her."11 The RPD asked him why he had not mentioned that he had been treated at the clinic as well. The Appellant responded, "Yes, I clearly remember that I had stated in my narrative that I had to go to the clinic. I don't know how that part got omitted from the narrative."12
Although I find this is a relatively minor inconsistency, I agree with the RPD's finding that it was not adequately explained. Delay in departure not fatal

I agree with the RPD that the short delay between the last incident on XXXX XXXX 2018 and the Appellant's departure from Bangladesh on XXXX XXXX 2018 is not fatal to his claim. However, contrary to the RPD, I draw no adverse inference from the fact that the Appellant hid at his home during this period. This is because the RPD did not ask him to explain why he hid at home rather than hiding somewhere else. Findings with regard to availability of phone number for the police are speculative

I find the RPD erred in drawing a negative inference from the fact that the Appellant had not called the police during the XXXX 2017 attack. This is because the RPD's finding that the number for the local police station was easily available is speculative in light of the documentation which shows there was no emergency number for the police at the relevant time.13 No inconsistency between BOC and testimony respecting conversation of XXXX XXXX 2018

I also find the RPD erred in drawing a negative inference from the Appellant's omission of a conversation with the agent of persecution that occurred at the time of the XXXX XXXX 2018 attack. I find it is clear from the narrative that there was more than a "one-line verbal exchange".14 While the Appellant provided more detail in testimony,15 I see no obvious inconsistencies. I draw no adverse inference on this particular point. Medical documentation from XXXX 2018 too vague to be given any weight

The RPD gave the medical documents respecting the XXXX 2018 assault no weight as it found the description of his injuries, ("seriously injured and body aches") as well as the treatment, ("major medicine used in health complex") were vague.16 I find the RPD correctly determined that these documents were too vague to be given any weight. Lawyer's letter, complainant's statement and FIR do not support allegations

With regard to the false charges brought against the Appellant, the RPD correctly noted that the complainant's statement17 and the First Information Report (FIR)18 do not identify the agent of persecution as the complainant. When asked how he knew the agent of persecution was involved in bringing charges against him, the Appellant's explanation was that he did not have problems with anyone else.19 I find no error in the RPD rejecting this explanation and drawing a negative inference with respect to the FIR.

I also agree with the RPD that the Appellant's lawyer's letter20 is lacking in details that could reasonably be expected, such as what the Appellant has actually been charged with or whether an arrest warrant has been issued. The RPD further noted the Appellant's lack of knowledge regarding these charges.21 The RPD correctly determined that these issues undermined the credibility of the Appellant's allegations. Lack of letter from the Appellant's father

The RPD drew a further negative inference as the Appellant had not provided a letter from his father, who was the principal target in the extortion attempts by the agents of persecution. The Appellant explained that he did not want to ask his father or add to his problems by asking for a letter.22 However, the Appellant did not explain why asking for a letter would pose such a problem. Particularly, since the Appellant did obtain other documents from his father such as his father's complaint to the police.23 The RPD did not err in this regard. Remaining documentation insufficient to overcome credibility concerns

The RPD correctly noted that none of the affiants who had provided supporting affidavits had witnessed any of the alleged events firsthand.24 All were based on information provided by the Appellant's family. Further, the affidavit of AO indicates that the police refused to take a complaint25 which directly contradicts the FIR filed by the Appellant's father.26

I have also considered the medical report from XXXX 2017.27 However, even accepting this report at face value, there is nothing which links this assault to the Appellant's father or to extortion by government agents.

Finally, considered the letter from the President of the XXXX XXXX XXXX.28 However, in my assessment, the statements contained in this letter - specifically that the government, Members of Parliament and Ministers are involved in the attacks on the Appellant's father - are simply not supported by any evidence.
I find that none of this documentation can be given any weight.

Considering all of the above, I find that the Appellant failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, the core allegations upon which his claim is based. This is fatal to his claim whether considered under section 96 or 97 of Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). I therefore reject this appeal.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a), I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
